newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS-12 Mexican pension firms prepare for battle.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-12 Mexican pension firms prepare for battle.

text.p: Mexico on Tuesday gave the go-ahead to its first 12 private pension management firms to launch operations, paving the way for a scramble to snag an early lead in an industry that will revolutionize savings.

The 12 firms, many a mixture of Mexican and foreign capital, can start advertising and signing up customers next month, according to Fernando Solis, head of the government's National Retirement Saving System Commission (Consar).
Five others have sought another month to prepare for final approval from the Consar, including the government pension, called Afore XXI, controlled by the Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS).

Solis told a news conference the approved Afores, as the funds are known in Mexico, can begin advertising on Feb. 1, and can start the crucial task of affiliating workers two days later -- giving them up to a one-month headstart over their five remaining rivals.

In factories and businesses, however, many among Mexico's 10 million insured workers are expected to be wary of the unprecedented sales drive, especially in a country where many banks have come close to collapse in the last two years.

Mexico's private banks are among the main shareholders of the Afores, and they are expected to have an uphill struggle convincing workers to entrust to them their nest eggs, however paltry returns were under the previous social security scheme.
Solis clamped a list of restrictions on Afores to ensure that they do not win over workers unscrupulously. For example, promotional gifts such as lighters and key rings were banned.

Also, Afores were prohibited from giving incentives to union bosses to encourage them to bring their members en bloc into one pension fund management firm. "Workers are free to choose whichever Afore is most suitable," Solis said.

In the early stages, two Afores are expected to make the running. They are Afore Banamex, run single-handedly by Mexico's largest banking group Grupo Financiero Banamex-Accival, and Afore Bancomer, a joint venture of Grupo Financiero Bancomer and U.S.-based Aetna.

Both Mexican banks, the giants of the shaky system, already control the lion's share of pensions under a soon-to-be-disbanded system in which pensions are collected by the state and partly managed by private banks. The two Afores were among the 12 given the go-ahead by the Consar.

Financial analysts say that by sheer inertia they may come close to winning the upper limit of 17 percent of total affiliations within a year of the launch of private pension fund management in September.

Other Afores are already chomping at the bit to get into the race. On Tuesday, one of the hottest-tipped competitors, Profuturo GNP Afore, which combines Mexican insurer Grupo Nacional Provincial, Chile's Provida and Spain's Banco Bilbao Vizcaya, said it aimed to attract 1.5 million workers in its first year.

With a sales force of 4,000, it aims to target middle and lower-income workers, visiting as many as possible of the 10 million potential affiliates individually and launching an agressive advertising campaign to tout its advantages.
Workers have four years to choose which Afore they want to begin with, and at least 15 percent are expected to begin by taking the government option, Afore XXI.
President Ernesto Zedillo hopes the pension reforms will provide a vital boost to savings in Mexico, which will spur economic growth and add depth to the country's capital markets.

But the new scheme has proven costly to a cash-strapped government, that estimates it needs to sink some 0.5 percent of GDP into getting it off the ground this year alone. Eyeing the fiscal pressure, the government has already put back its launch by seven months to September.
